utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just as a reminder to the Chamber, Exhibit 378, tab 5, is on the overhead projector, and that's a summary of some of this portion of Mr. Kirudja's testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, when we concluded your testimony last week, you were describing a report of an incident regarding a large number of people detained in the football stadium in Bosanski Novi on the 6th of June, 1992. Before I move forward from that point, is there any point or detail which you would like to add to what you've told us so far about that incident?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not any that I have presently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution 378, tab 7. Mr. Kirudja, as with the other exhibits, I'd ask you to look over it. And I'd ask that the second page of the exhibit be placed on the overhead projector. I would ask you, Mr. Kirudja, do you recognise Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 7?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a memorandum that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this memorandum, is one of the things that you write about the Bosanski Novi football stadium incident?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the 3rd of July, were there other memos in which you had referenced this report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among other reports of refugees crossing into Sector North.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say -- or can you tell us, the report of the Bosanski Novi football stadium incident, was that a restricted report or were other members of your office and the UN generally, did they have access to that report as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you note, this memorandum carries the word "restricted" at the top right-hand corner, yet if you look at the end of that memorandum, it also indicates to whom the memorandum is addressed. The meaning of "restricted" is that it's restricted to those people to which the memorandum is addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the witness be handed the last page of the exhibit. It doesn't need to be on the overhead. Please leave that page on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, can you tell us who this memorandum was sent to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, it's addressed to Mrs. Yolanda Auger who was the deputy director of civil affairs, and it was also copied to a Mr. Magnusson in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, the first page of this memorandum is on the overhead projector. I would ask you to read for us the third paragraph, the paragraph beginning with, "We believe..."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We believe the football field detainees are only a tip of the iceberg involving the concerted action of local Serbian authorities in BH trying to establish a Serbian Republic of BH, free of Muslims. In that process, the mayors, the milicija and TDF of Bosanski Novi, acting in unison with their counterparts, not only in the UNPA (Dvor and Kostajnica), but also with Bosanska Dubica, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc. The Serbs appear to be engaged in a determined process of forcefully disarming Muslims where they are clearly a small encircled minority, such as in Bosanski Novi, or besieging their city totally, such as in Bihac. Apparently the football field is the holding ground where Muslim groups are detained while their houses are being 'searched,' the men isolated and transported to concentration camps." End of quote of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to please continue on to the bottom portion where you actually list a number of suspected concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continuing, and I quote: "The UNHCR representative and Civil Affairs have pieced together reports from Muslims who recently have taken refuge under UNPROFOR protection in Dvor and Kostajnica. There are reported concentration camps at the following locations. "Keraterm: Located at a railroad station in Prijedor en route to Banja Luka. 100-200 Muslims believed to be here under extremely bad conditions. "Trnopolje: Also located at a railroad station in Prijedor, direction Banja Luka. A refugee camp for women, children, and old men." Do you want me to read the second page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Omarska: Located in a purely Serbian village. Reportedly a camp for Muslim men and local Muslim authorities prior to Serbian takeover of control, particularly in Prijedor. "Manjaca: Outside Banja Luka. A large camp reportedly including Croatian soldiers taken prisoner in the fighting in Kostajnica."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you just to finish with the next sentence and conclude your reading there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The treatment of Muslims and other minorities in the camps is reportedly atrocious, with regular beatings, deprivation of food and water, poor shelter, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I want to ask you a few questions regarding this memo. In the first paragraph, you used the word "milicija." Could you please define that for us.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Milicija" is a term I learned to associate with regular police, those of the military camouflage form in distinction from regular fighting forces in camouflage uniforms. The police wore blue and were regularly referred to as "milicija."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the milicija exist post demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in particular in the UNPA post demobilisation, the milicija in the camouflage uniforms became increasingly blended and harder to distinguish one from the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned several locations. Dvor and Kostajnica, what country is that in?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dvor and Kostajnica were at that time part of the UNPA inside what is now Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Bosanski Dubica, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc, where are they located?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are across the border into what is now Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us the type of sources that you used to generate this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- could I ask the usher to put the previous exhibit on, and we're finished with that one. Thank you. And that's Exhibit 5 -- tab 5.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. This memorandum we just finished talking about has a paragraph referring to many previous memorandums on the same subject. I take your question to our sources inclusive of those references to other reports of similar kind. This was as a result of people coming -- this particular memorandum, we used to have people, a stream of refugees, coming into the sector and seeking protection. And as we provided that protection, we would talk to them as to why and where they were coming from and what caused them to flee. So this particular memorandum was done after a number, I forget the exact number of all night refugees coming into the sector, interviewed by my -- by my people plus the civil police, and compiling the summary we have read, where they were fleeing from and why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an estimate of the number of primary sources, these refugees, who would have made reports that eventually would have ended up in a summary report of this fashion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A clarification: The refugees themselves didn't make the report. Our staff talking to the refugees debriefed them and then they found their way into our concerted report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are we talking about dozens of people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate of approximately how many people would have gone into a summary report of this nature?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this one, I wouldn't be surprised if there would be almost a hundred or so. I'm not sure of the exact number. As I mentioned, we were engaged for almost all day, all night talking to these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask now a different exhibit be placed on the overhead, and that is Exhibit 378, tab 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being done, Mr. Kirudja, may I ask you, on the 6th of July, 1992, did you receive a letter from someone?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the Serbian be placed on the overhead and the English translation given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the letter, and it is -- yes, I did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I'd ask if the director could zoom out so we could see the entire -- perhaps if it could be shifted on the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this letter from?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from Radomir Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he sign the letter as the mayor of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he sign the letter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crisis Committee President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us the circumstances under which you received this letter and its contents.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had come to my office in one of two or three meetings. I -- this one may have been received in the second or third meeting in our office where he sought to convince us, and me in particular, of why we should agree with this proposal to transition 5.000 refugees through Sector North.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to just look at the original or the facsimile of the document on the overhead projector. Do you recognise the signature and the seal that is affixed to it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a signature and a seal, and since it was the first time I had seen it, I wouldn't know whether any more that it -- but it looked official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does this letter contain the following? Does this letter say that a large number of people want to leave Bosanski Novi, and does it claim they have been issued the necessary paperwork allowing them to leave?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for the specific part where that language is. I'm sorry, I don't see the specific language that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, in your own words, to summarise the content of the letter that you received.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a -- this letter pretty much summarises what I received verbally and -- from him, the gist of what he explained in greater detail when he was talking to us, and that had to do with why he considered that the people were leaving voluntarily from Bosanski Novi and the status of an agreement he had reached with them so that they could leave voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does he identify the bus companies, the names of the bus companies with which he's made arrangements to transport these people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does he also indicate to you what arrangements have been made for an escort for these buses containing these supposed voluntary refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did he make arrangements with regarding that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Companies Kozaraprevoz, Autoprevoz Dvor, and private vehicles and other means of transportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was to escort these buses?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The escorting would be by the "Republic of Serbian Krajina workers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mention anything about the Ministry of Internal Affairs? I draw your attention to the third to last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the institution providing internal affairs of Republic of Serbian Krajina workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit. I'd ask that the summary page tab 5 once again be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, Mr. Kirudja, did you -- did the deputy mayor Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of Bosanski Novi and the mayor of Dvor again request that 5.000 Muslims be allowed to leave the area voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 18th of July, did you receive a directive from your superior regarding your observations of what was going on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a directive from my superiors in Zagreb not to be involved with what was going on in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you respond to that directive?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was rather sad, though the directive was not unexpected. I was disappointed by it because it took -- it took a bureaucratic approach into what we were saying, that we were receiving refugees under -- we were responding to people in dire need not from Bosnia-Herzegovina but from where we were located legitimately by the mission, and yet my headquarters saw that as "involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina." That was extremely disappointing to me, and I made it clear to them that we were not exceeding our concern, we were responding to people in need who were drawn to where we were by the fact that the UN flag was flying above us. As a result, I called my staff and confirmed to them we were not going to stop from reporting and responding to these people as they came to us. We owed it to tell to our headquarters and beyond that these people are coming, under what circumstances, and in what conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you in fact continue to report on events in Bosnia as they impacted on your work in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the later part of July, the 21st of July. Did the government of Croatia in fact agree to accept 4.000 of the Bosanski Novi refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that was true, and I must add they agreed after a long period of resisting the idea themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe what happened after the Croatian government agreed to allow these people to enter Croatia proper?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, all that was left was to see to it that the 4.000 that was requested were treated properly and given all the support that they needed to safely come out of the sector into that part of Croatia that the sector bordered, that is, outside the sector into Croatian official control areas, at Karlovac specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did 4.000 people in fact leave Bosanski Novi and travel through Sector North on to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't 4.000; it turned out to be more like 9.000 plus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position regarding future similar evacuations related to what you believed was ethnic cleansing? Did you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, as soon as this -- this matter was clearly understood both by my headquarters, UNHCR and ICRC, and following that transit by 9.000, we sought to make it clearer to them that this is the beginning. If you allow it, it is going to be a flood and, therefore, we continuously tried to give them to understand what we knew, and I'm glad to report they did turn around and joined - I mean "they" meaning UNHCR, ICRC - they did turn around to our position that this is an affair we couldn't be involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time now, Mr. Kirudja, I would ask you to look at Prosecution 378, tab 9. I would ask that the first page be placed on the overhead and that you take the second page. And I'll ask you a few questions regarding the report in general and then about it in particular. I'd ask you just to review the subject, the date, and the author of the memo, and then I'd ask you whether you recognise this memo.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a memorandum prepared and authored by one of my assistants called Mr. Paolo Raffone, a civil affairs officer based in my office and reporting to me, and it is also released under my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your signature appears on that document as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the first paragraph on the second page, the page you have. I'd ask you to read that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph reads as follows, and I quote: "A calculated strategy to 'cleanse' the area of Muslims appears to have intensified beginning in May 1992. House burnings, deportations, summary executions, shooting in the houses, et cetera, are a part of the present situation in the towns and villages along the north side of the BH border (Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Kostajnica, and Bosanska Dubica. Reportedly, the milicija does not seem to intervene. Some mayors and other Serbs working in other opstinas have also been reported as trying to help the Muslims to leave their houses safely. In Bosanski Novi, the military police is reported to have its HQ in Hotel Una. There are reports of brutal torture in this hotel." End of quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, are you able to tell us what would be the source of information of this report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same source of stream of people arriving in the sector and being interviewed before being given safe transit outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. I'd ask that tab 5 once again be placed on the overhead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I want to draw your attention now to some other areas, different than Bosanski Novi, and ask you some specific questions about them. And the areas I want to draw your attention to now are Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most, and Banja Luka. On the 1st of June 1992, did Mr. Kupresanin, the mayor of Banja Luka, make a report or have a conversation with your office regarding the situation of Muslims in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a telephone call received by Mr. Raffone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe what occurred.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a telephone call that Raffone took and made note of what he was being told by the mayor of Banja Luka. And the mayor of Banja Luka, the gist of what he told him was to the effect that there were already 15.000 refugees already leaving the area in the towns that you have mentioned, namely Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kljuc, and Bosanski Dubica, and that there would be 15.000 more to follow, and that he pleaded that United Nations, the UNHCR, these people needed assistance from them. That was the gist of his call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kupresanin, do you know what his ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to other municipalities, Velika Kladusa and Bosanska Krupa. Are they in Bosnia as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Velika Kladusa and Bosanska Dubica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, did the Serb deputy mayor of Dvor notify you regarding the presence of refugees in the Croatian town of Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On what day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of June. Yes. My notes do reflect that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to draw your attention -- I'd actually ask you to open to page, in your notebooks, to this date, the 12th of August, 1992. My question to you is: As the initial group of 9.000 refugees from Bosanski Novi, were there attempts to move additional refugees from that area through Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 12th of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And confirming our greatest fears that the 9.000 wouldn't be the last ones, the meeting on this date did underscore our greatest fear on this regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- or did the Serb mayor give you a warning on that day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came in this time that they were requesting more refugees, would assist them to do -- to do the same thing as had happened previously with the 9.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he make any statement to you what would occur if he was left to have to resolve this matter by himself? I would draw your attention, during the preparation of your testimony, I asked you to place a green tab next to the portion that I'm interested in at this point.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And it was kind of a warning to us if we didn't do what they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read -- do you have a quote?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you record a quote? Could you please read that to us.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote that: "If the Serbian side is not respected, there could be massive deaths on both sides. If we are left to resolve the matter by ourselves, we will resolve the matter very quickly. For example, there are 7.000 Serb refugees from Croatia in Bosanski Novi. The world did not condemn their plight."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that passage, the latter part of that passage, he's referring to Serbs in Croatia that were made refugees by events there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in late June of 1992, did you also receive reports of the expulsion or harassment of Croats by Serb authorities and armed persons within Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where specifically?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this was a group of five, I believe, five Croats that had been forcibly moved out of their houses somewhere south of Korenica into Sector North, and then we had them housed in a hotel in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 21st of July, 1992, did you report to your superiors the existence of 10.000 non-Serb refugees from the area of Bihac in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We alluded to reports reaching us of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 12th of August of 1992, did Bosnian Serbs request that the UN evacuate 500 non-Serb refugees from Bosanska Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was among the numbers in the meeting I just quoted from -- in Bosanski Novi. We had been given a list of possible refugees in a number of places, and that was one of them named, and the figure of 500 given as potential refugees from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the second week in August, did you have an estimate of how many non-Serb refugees sought to flee Bosnia by travelling through Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they started looking for the second round of numbers to be evacuated through Sector North, the numbers started at 5.000. By the end of the period you're referring to, the number had swelled to 28.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, up until this point, all the communications you had regarding the evacuation of these people, it was always with Serb mayors or Serb officials; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bottom end of that process, it started with the Serb officials, but immediately we had to keep the Croatian side involved in the matter because they would have to be taken through the sector into the waiting hands of the Croatian side. So we dealt with the bottom of the process with the Serbs, at the end of the process with the Croats, but flipping back and forth between the two groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking is, up until this point, the meetings and the phone calls and the letters, were they all from Serbs or were they from -- did you ever have a meeting in which Muslims attended, prior to August?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In one meeting that Mr. Pasic and his group had requested of me, he had brought two Muslims in his team to tell us about the nature of this. Other than that, we were -- nobody else was involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that meeting held on the 19th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So prior to the 19th of August, no Muslim had ever come to your office, requesting voluntary removal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And not even since. And they came in the company of the Serb group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to this meeting, you estimate that at least 28.000 had become refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 28.000 was the projected figure in an attempt for a second round after the 9.000 had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about that meeting. Can you tell us in a little bit more detail who attended that meeting of the 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of August, I had Mr. Vrkes, Vlado Vrkes, who had the title as the president of SDS of Sanski Most; Mr. Majkic, Dragan Majkic, who was the representative of the milicija of Sanski Most; Mr. Islamcevic, Besim Islamcevic, who was a representative of Muslim and Croatian willing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to leave Sanski Most, the person I referred to as the only one of two Muslims; Mr. Asanovic, Esad Asanovic, who was the representative of Muslim refugees from Bosanska Krupa, now in Sanski Most. I also, of course, had other -- had the representatives of UNHCR in my office in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of this meeting, were you requested to assist in the evacuation of specific numbers of non-Serbs from specific municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I ask you just to tell us the municipality and the number that you were requested to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers came in two parts. One I was told in total. I was told in total, Sanski Most, they expected 11.000 applicants to leave. Bosanski Krupa, 600 applicants. Prijedor, 8.000 applicants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also presented with something at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To my surprise, it was a computer list printed in the kind of a -- the old printer, computer printer where you fold one after another, and you folded it - it was about the size of this book - containing lists of names of the applicants themselves and complete details. And now, since I don't have a copy of that report, I'm just working on memory. It was nicely printed but it had more than details of the names. It totalled -- after they left, we went through the names and it totalled somewhere around 7.700 plus of the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was presented to you as these are the people that we want you to help leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your reaction to having been given that list?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A shock. We had already gone through this. We had already told them our incredulity about the claim that people could be voluntarily leaving their homes. It didn't seem to register. And now they seemed to have worked on it very meticulously about who it is. I must say, when I -- I got a little reminder of something that happened in the Second World War, about trying to remove people and going about it meticulously, which is one of the reasons why I mentioned earlier I had to tell my staff we couldn't not tell this story, notwithstanding the directive I had received from my headquarters not to be involved in it. It is in my office we are talking about, inside the UNPA, not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form an impression regarding the level of organisation between Serbs on both the Croatian -- on the Croatian side of the border and the Bosnian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Impression?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Impression. When you were presented with this list, did you form an impression whether there was a sophisticated level of organisation between the Serb leaders on the Croatian side and the Serb leaders on the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it gave me a mixed conflicting understanding. On one side, even if we told them in no uncertain terms how wrong this was, there seemed to be a level, unfortunately I used the word naivete about it, and they didn't seem really to be perturbed, and it didn't look more like devious, it was just there was a strict naivete about it and not even trying to understand it, a kind of refusal to understand it on the one side. On the other side, they seemed to be pretty determined to pull it through as to prepare all of this, and the persistent nature in which they sought our agreement to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continuing through September of 1992, was there a steady stream of Bosnian refugees making their way into Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before I conclude this portion of your testimony, I want to -- I forgot to ask you a question regarding the letter from the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Pasic, and I can have the exhibit shown to you again if you require. Did he sign his name as the mayor of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how he signed his name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: President of the Crisis Committee, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of that title before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask that Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 10, be placed on the overhead projector. I'd just point out a correction for the Chamber. This is in fact pages 26 and 27 from Prosecution Exhibit 336, the map book, and it's a photocopy. The summary says pages 20 and 21. That's incorrect. It's 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, do you recognise what is depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the director zoom out a little bit so we can get the two municipalities on the top. A little more. Very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, I'd ask you, did you make the markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you just to walk us through the markings and just briefly describe what each marking indicates.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the fact that this is the border. This is the international border of Bosnia and the -- this is there, the internationally recognised border. As you'll see, all of these areas that are marked are well -- either at the border or well inside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were operating from inside, on the other side of the border, and this stream of the people was going up into the sector through this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kirudja, would I be correct in saying that Dvor is the only Croatian municipality that you've circled on this map?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please start from the left-hand side of the map, just identify the location and tell us what your markings indicate.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Bihac town, and we have marked around 10.000 estimated refugees in that -- from that area and coming through Bihac. Bosanski Krupa. The 600 estimate was given to me in my office as we have just talked about in that meeting of 19th of August. Then Sanski Most. The 11.000 estimated, again from that meeting in my office. There was some to come from Kljuc, but I don't recall if there was any particular estimate or the number. Then Banja Luka. This is where the telephone call I referred to taken by my assistant took -- was taken from, where the mayor was warning us and requesting assistance and telling us 15.000 have left and 15.000 may be coming thereafter. This is Prijedor, where the number of 8.000 was given in my office as potentially coming from that town. And this is Bosanski Kostajnica. Again this is on the border town with Croatia and we had a presence also on the other side and where the number of 500 was estimated from. This is again another border town, Bosanski Dubica, where we were also given notice that the refugees would be coming from there. I have circled the small thing. In the memorandum that you made me read a few minutes ago, I mentioned a number of places where we were told that there were refugees, and Omarska was one of them, and that is where I've circled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit, thank you. Now, Mr. Kirudja, leaving the evacuations related to ethnic cleansing, I want to bring you back to the mayor of Vrginmost, Mr. Obradovic. You've mentioned him earlier in your testimony. Could you tell us what happened to Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic one morning - I recall that it was Saturday but it was a morning around 9.00 - was killed in a stretch of the road between Vrginmost and Topusko, a wooded area. He was ambushed there and was shot several times from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the scene of the shooting that day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almost an hour or so within that period, I was there. It's a very short distance from where we were located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself personally make attempts to medevac, or evacuate, him by helicopter to a larger hospital?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went from the scene of the crime. He didn't die on the scene. He had been evacuated to a local hospital and they were attempting to save his life when they also requested we give them a medevac on -- to save his life as they were frantically trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened with respect to those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, we told them that it would be easier for us to give him evacuation, but the evacuation, since we were in Topusko, our helicopters would take him to Zagreb, which was actually a short distance away from where we were, but they turned that down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They turned that down first because their insistence that the medevac be to Belgrade, which was quite a distance from there. And before we could even reach an agreement on that, around 2.00, Mr. Obradovic, unfortunately, died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an investigation into how -- the circumstances surrounding Mr. -- Mayor Obradovic's death?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after, even while he was on the hospital, trying to save his life, there were many roadblocks erected immediately, and this was in the operational zone of Kordun. So the military units of Kordun and Cedo Bulat and the police and Mr. -- the police, Djuro Skaljac, they went into high gear trying to catch who they called Croatian infiltrators. Immediately I was told there were Croatian infiltrators all over the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you believe that Mr. Obradovic was killed by Croatian infiltrators?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. There were many reasons for me to discount any Croatian infiltrators. Not that there weren't any. There had been in the past reasons to suppose there were Croatian infiltrators, but not on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion, there were many, many curious things that happened. I mentioned I was in the hospital with only one or two officials and that the most high ranking official in that hospital was Mile Paspalj. He came wearing a gun for the first time himself. And as I talked to them, it was clear that they were much more worried about something among themselves than something outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you believe was responsible for the death of Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't sure, nor was I ever able to find out despite my -- I had pretty good sources of people who advised and gave me an idea of the direction if not the detail of something as magnitude as that, but they all froze. Nobody would even dare to talk to me about that. Secondly, if they really believed in Croatian infiltrators, I would not hear the end of it, not just a week later but thereafter they would have made clear to the Croatian side. So the story of the Croatian infiltrators rose one day and disappeared immediately. So all in all, it was clear that there was terror among the Serbs themselves in that area about this death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber briefly what Mr. Obradovic's political disposition would have been.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic was a quiet - and I emphasise this - quiet in relative to the other mayors who were given to a lot of speech-making, political kind, about national -- living together in one country. He was a quiet man. He also was given to interpreting the Vance Plan precisely the way it was intended to, and that was it gave the mayor and the chief of police the only authority recognised, and he seemed to play up to that that way. In short, there was an air of independence, a quiet independence around him, and he got about doing his business that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what was the effect of his death among the other Serb political leaders in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chill, a real chill, a noticeable one. And not long thereafter, several of them did quit and were new mayors, particularly in Dvor itself. And in Vojnic there was a new mayor put in over there. And I believe mostly in those two places. And apart from the chill, there was changes in the mayor personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So mayors were actually replaced.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly in those two places, in Dvor and Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described last week for us that the highest level of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. government, local government, not counting the signatories on the Vance Plan, but the highest level of local government was at the municipality level.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Recognised by the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Recognised by the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did his murder have some change on the role that Knin played with respect to the operation of local governments at the municipality level?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I underscore the role of Knin was pronounced not long after we arrived in April or May. He was killed -- I forget the date. It was much later. The role of Knin now became more pronounced. The difference that mayors gave and police officers gave to Knin became total at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in an unrelated matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go on to that, what roughly is the date of the murder of the mayor? Have we got some idea?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate for us or do you have it in your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's somewhere, but it's not present in my mind -- I know it was a Saturday morning, that was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt in due course we can be told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can tell you that later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you, during one of the breaks, to please review your notebooks and I will ask you later on.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April of 1993, did you become aware of an incursion from Croatia from the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the one into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe where into Bosnia these troops went.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the border, that international border I referred to a little earlier, there is a stretch of that border running between the town of Velika Kladusa and Bihac. That particular stretch of the border was turbulent, and we had military observers on both sides; in Velika Kladusa and in Bihac. The Serbs made an incursion across into the area behind Velika Kladusa after three hours of artillery bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you about Mr. Fikret Abdic. Do you know who he is, and did you have occasion to meet with him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mr. Abdic and met with him quite frequently, a number of times. He was based in Velika Kladusa, and we had a lot of these military issues and humanitarian issues that affected that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Chamber who he was.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, on the one hand, he was a politician, a member of the Presidency in Sarajevo, and attempted and lost an election that he made clear, he reminded us many times, that he had won that election. In other words, a politician, a member of the Presidency. On the other hand, he was also a businessman and the head of one of the largest agri-business, known as Agrokomerc, based in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever describe for you an agreement he had reached with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And again, out of the agenda. We were there to talk about something else, about incursions, some cease-fires between that, and he set aside the agenda on that occasion and started to talk to us about what he called the Belgrade declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he tell you when the Belgrade declaration was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 22nd of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to just open up to that page in your notes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had met on 26th of October in Maljevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he describe for you what the substance of this agreement he had made with President Milosevic was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me preface my answer in saying we were trying to solve a border incursion between the Serbs on the one side and the Muslims on the other, and once he pulled out the Belgrade declaration, there was a reason for him to put that. He believed it was the formula for ending any and all kinds of conflicts between the Muslims and the Serbs as an example of why we had come there to talk about that specific cease-fire. And he said after the Belgrade declaration, we have created the conditions for solving the Bosanska Bojna, Gradina issue - that is the issue that brought us there that day - we should start the process with a lot of confidence. Many documents were signed in the past. Unfortunately, none were fulfilled. I'm really ready to fulfil this declaration, meaning the Belgrade declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he indicate to you whether Mr. -- that the Belgrade declaration was an actual piece of paper that he signed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, my notes indicate two things. He was telling us the status of the declaration as of that point, but I also note that I was - and I recall seeing the broad elements of that agreement, but it was not by -- the details were not directly from Fikret but from his assistant, a man by the name Mr. Sajso [phoen]. But Mr. Abdic himself mentioned to me, and I quote from my notes here: "Pretty soon a meeting with Karadzic which I will have and I will host. I talked to Mr. Milosevic today by telephone. He promised to contact Karadzic for this purpose." Now, from the note of the general parameters I understood of this declaration, it also had the agreement of Mr. Tudjman. So basically, it did illustrate Mr. Fikret Abdic's bigger vision that he claimed and he made clear to us as representatives of the UN. And, generally summarised, was if he, Mr. Abdic, was in charge, he could end these fightings that were between Muslims and Croats and all of that because he could obtain an agreement easily or, rather, relatively easily with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Karadzic on the Serb side and Mr. Tudjman on the Croatian side and himself as a representative of the Muslims. And to illustrate that, he had created an area called the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia where he could illustrate his vision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to make sure that we understand what you've just told us, at the time you're meeting with Mr. Abdic, he's telling you that there is an existing agreement between himself and Mr. Milosevic that has the approval of Mr. Tudjman and that that very day Mr. Milosevic called Fikret Abdic --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he would call and arrange for Karadzic to visit Bihac so that he would also participate in this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Come on board on this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you later learned the details of the agreement between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Abdic from Mr. Abdic's assistant. Are there any details which you have not described so far? If you haven't, I would ask you to tell us any additional details of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have given you from my notes the framework of how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this time, was there a level of cooperation between Colonel Bulat and Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was before then and after, a major, major collaboration between Fikret Abdic and Cedo Bulat on the Kordun side as well as Tarbuk on Banja side. I mentioned earlier the reason the meeting was held was an incursion into Bosanska Bojna by the Serbs, and it caused a major rift. That collaboration was to assist Fikret Abdic, ironically, fight his own Muslim group in Bihac in the form of the 5th Corps of Bihac that he had got into fighting relationship with, and he was getting the military support from Cedo Bulat as well as Tarbuk on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your view, did this agreement amount to a cease-fire of the fighting that was going on in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was better than a cease-fire. They had agreed on a complete pull-back from that area of Bosnia where the Serbs had gone in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us it was an agreement between Mr. Milosevic, Abdic, with the approval of -- I want to ask you, there was any mention about a member of the federal government of Yugoslavia, of their involvement in this agreement or their having signed an agreement with Mr. Abdic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your forbearance in misunderstanding you when I was talking about an agreement. It's obvious from your last comment that you are talking about Belgrade declaration. I was not talking about Belgrade declaration, I was talking about a parallel agreement about a pull-back in the region in an area called Bosanska Bojna. Now, to repeat, that had nothing to do with Belgrade. So could you kindly rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Belgrade declaration that you've referred to, did that result in a cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't look to it itself had a direct role. There was something else that ended the hostilities locally there that had nothing to do with the Belgrade declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please describe that for us.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a concerted effort between the UN and the Serb side and Fikret Abdic to locally disengage. The Serbs themselves were -- ended up conceding it was an error and they needed to get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, back to the Belgrade declaration. Was there ever any mention of the involvement or role that the federal government of Yugoslavia had to play in this agreement with Abdic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abdic himself made it clear he just needed their support of his idea of Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. From there on, he made it clear he was capable of taking care of the area himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the federal government of the Bosnian government, I'm talking about of Yugoslavia itself.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood, and my reply was he made clear that he needed the endorsement from Belgrade of his Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. He needed and got endorsement from Tudjman. He needed and got an endorsement -- or rather, was working to get Karadzic, through Belgrade, to agreed to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you conclude your duties in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the two years. It's normal to end the duties around that time, and it was around 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you were transferred to Belgrade to take up other responsibilities for the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was transferred after a short stint in Zagreb in the capacity of civil affairs Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your title when you served in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title was the delegate of the special representative of the Secretary-General, who at that time was Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately when did you assume your duties there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date probably is August 1994 or somewhere around that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what your duties entailed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was to be -- to have a big component of that responsibility was to help Mr. -- the diplomatic communications between the headquarters of UNPROFOR and Mr. Akashi's headquarters and the government in Belgrade. There was a big diplomatic component in that assignment

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber, what procedure would you follow if there was an issue that Mr. Akashi wanted raised -- wanted you to raise with the Yugoslav authorities. What procedure would you follow, and please tell us how you would come to meet the people you came to meet.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was well-executed procedure that worked pretty well. There was a commission for relationship with UNPROFOR that was part of the Foreign Affairs Ministry of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At that time there was a Foreign Minister by the name of Jovanovic, and the commission itself had a secretary by the name of Mr. Pesut. If Mr. Akashi or Mr. De Mello or anyone wanted some diplomatic communication, a meeting set, I was requested to inform Mr. Pesut, as the secretary of that commission, that such-and-such meeting was requested for such-and-such a reason, and he would then contact the people requested and the meeting would be set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Jovanovic determine who were the people you should meet, depending upon the issues that you needed to raise?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely. Although, I had the courtesy and pleasure and the opportunity of meeting with Mr. Jovanovic, I didn't need that. I -- Mr. Pesut alone was enough to communicate the request. And even if it was a request for a meeting with the President of Serbia, at that time Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many meetings did you have with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am guessing around six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please tell us, just generally, the topics that you would have discussed with him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings were meetings requested by Mr. Akashi, and they covered the full range of the issues that UNPROFOR was engaged in, be it in Bosnia, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or those United Nations Protected Areas or issues specifically that were in the territory of the Rump Yugoslavia, meaning Serbia and Montenegro. And those were the issues of the Prevlaka peninsula in Montenegro or Resolution 781 that dealt with the no-fly that was imposed on the former Yugoslavia, and monitors were watching the flights out of Serbian skies, searching in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you generally characterise your interaction with Mr. Milosevic during these meetings.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very professional, and I will take the opportunity to recognise he was always very kind and courteous, and we -- we had his reaction in time as well -- as well as in substance as the -- as Mr. Akashi wished. In other words, at no time was there a request by Mr. Akashi that was turned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to several of those meetings, and the first one I'd like to draw your attention to is on the 26th of October of 1994 regarding an unofficial meeting with Mr. Milosevic to discuss the FRY's position towards the conflict in BiH. Do you have a clear recollection of that meeting or would you like to refer to your notes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who else was in that meeting? Was it Mr. Akashi or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. De Mello was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This meeting was really -- yes, I recall it, and essentially it was an informal meeting. Not for the purpose you have mentioned, but it was the time when Mr. De Mello was ending his role in the former Yugoslavia, and it was a courtesy meeting to say farewell to the president at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the topic of the FRY's position towards the conflict in Bosnia arise?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that context, and I would like to be clear that it was in that context of two people, Mr. De Mello and Mr. Milosevic, kind of taking back a look at the issues that they had discussed earlier, and they covered a number of topics, including the one you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Milosevic characterise the position of the FRY towards the conflict in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He made it clear that the war solutions were not going to be producing any results, and he did speak at length about his quest for a peaceful outcome rather than a war outcome in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of that meeting, was there also some discussion with Mr. Milosevic regarding nationalists within Serbia and, in particular, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because he was -- to underscore his point about the option for peace and no option for war, he mentioned so-called hawks and hard-liners in Serbia who he said were waning in influence. Their influence was decreasing. And to give an example, he gave an example of Mr. Seselj at that time in the parliament of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and mentioned that his immunity had been withdrawn at that time so he could face some charges. He also mentioned that Seselj's - how do you say? - supporter or a leader, somebody who was aligned with Seselj in the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Knin, that person also had been removed, and that was Mr. Milosevic's way of underscoring to Mr. De Mello that the forces of peace were winning over the forces of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to another meeting approximately a month later, on the 23rd of November, 1994. Did you meet with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the substance of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is the meeting called by Mr. Akashi, and this was in the context of NATO action that had been brought to bear on an airport controlled by the Serbs called Udbina airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what of significance occurred during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was rather -- there was a measure of tension in the meeting because the military side of UNPROFOR and others -- and Mr. Martic were talking an issue that of course had resulted in airstrikes, and most of the meeting was taken up with Mr. Martic denying very much that this was something that they caused and kind of turning the tables the other way, that it was an aggression by NATO and that the people of the Serbian Republic were -- I mean, the people of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were very -- were on edge. They took offence on this, and he implied that he was doing his best to prevent these people from attacking UNPROFOR for these actions. So he spent a lot of time along those lines of complaints, meaning Martic, at the end of which he requested Mr. Akashi to condemn those strikes as a way of getting on the good side of Serb in the -- Serbs in the UNPA. All this time, Mr. Milosevic was listening and the conversation was not with him; it was with Mr. Martic up to a point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did at some point in the meeting Mr. Milosevic take a greater role in discussion at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After all that kind of point, counterpoint between the military side and the UN and Mr. Martic, Mr. Milosevic did intervene. Generally, if I recall correct, he did two things: He did associate himself with the feeling that the NATO action was uncalled for on the -- a point that Martic was making. On the one side, having conceded to Martic that he, Mr. Milosevic, agreed that NATO action was uncalled for, he also spoke to Martic kind of indirect by telling him what he believed his obligation was and that - Martic's obligation - and that was not to do things that resulted in the war option being exercised in this -- against the Serbs. Consistent with the point Mr. Milosevic had made many times about war and peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Groome. Let me get back to the earlier issue a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, let's go back to the issue of the removal of Seselj's men in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic say that he had done that himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't say he had done it himself but he said that in the process, things like were happening - example, there was the removal - without saying whether by himself or by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And one thing more: Could you explain the immunity which was -- had been given to Mr. Seselj. What was it like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of parliament, of the federal republic or parliament, I understood that to mean that you would be -- you have a certain measure of immunity from prosecution as long as you are a member of parliament. And in order to lay charges on him, that immunity was removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to a meeting on the 3rd of May, and the topic of the meeting -- I'm sorry, the 3rd of May, 1995, in which the topic of the meeting was Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me if you forbear with me on the earlier meeting. I mentioned there was a topic of strikes in Udbina. There was a second topic in which Mr. Milosevic intervened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second topic that came up in that meeting was a remark that Martic made about the Serb forces doing their best "to prevent humanitarian help going into Bihac." And that was Martic openly saying we have been trying to prevent humanitarian assistance going into the pocket of Bihac. At that point, that illustrated some things we'd been saying all along, that Bihac was besieged and no humanitarian effort was going in. At that point, at that remark by Martic, Mr. Milosevic did intervene to make clear in no uncertain terms, Mr. Martic, that such an action was not to be contemplated and that humanitarian assistance into the pocket had to be allowed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's nothing -- is there anything else you think is of significance from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, that is what comes to my mind now, but if I look at my notes, we could look at whatever else you want to look at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention now to the 3rd of May, 1995, a meeting with Mr. Milosevic during which Western Slavonia was discussed. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again it was requested by Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the topic of a military commission arise in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was again for -- a background quickly: This was on something the Croats had done called Operation West Sector or something like that, where they had taken military action against Sector West, the Serbs in Sector West. And that, of course, was received very traumatically by the rest of the Serbs in other areas because it kind of portended what would come eventually for all areas that the Serbs had occupied in Croatia. And Mr. Milosevic, of course, was, like others, not supportive of that military action by Croatia, and he spoke along those lines, and in general in BiH he revived a concept of -- earlier on that had been instituted called commission on disarmament or commission -- I need -- it was a disengagement commission, a military disengagement commission that he wanted revived to deal with issues such as military actions by one side against the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 11, be placed or given to the witness. I'd ask that the first page be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, during the course of that meeting, did Mr. Milosevic characterise his relationship with Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a reference to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did he characterise his relationship with Mr. Mladic -- or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I pick up this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Pick it up and read it if you need to.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or refer to your diaries as well if that's required.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I make reference in this memo to the fact that the border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia had been closed for all males from the RS, and this, I advised -- my interpretation of it was because of the action taken, it would have some implications, and one was reducing the number of refugees that would be coming across; and secondly, it would by initial bolster the relationship with Mr. Mladic by cutting off the rate of desertion from the BSA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the 3rd of May meeting, and I'll still be using that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exhibit so -- the 3rd of May meeting, did Mr. Milosevic also characterise his view of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again in a persistent wane of those he conceded as hard-liners and hawks defeating his strategy of finding a political solution, those two were in that category. He saw them in that category at that stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask that the second page of that exhibit be placed on the overhead, and, Mr. Kirudja, first let me ask you: This is a report that you had done regarding your meetings or your analysis of meetings with Mr. Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a specific time and period an analysis at that particular specific time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to read the top paragraph on the second page. "After the 5-hour meeting on 16 May with Frasure, all the top brass of the ruling SPS began to show up at President Milosevic's office in Belgrade, again presumably to be briefed about the negotiations. Among them was Radmilo Bogdanovic, the former Interior Minister and now president of the federal parliament's Committee on Serbian diaspora; Boris Jovic, president of the federal parliament's committee on foreign policy; and Milomir Minic, the Secretary-General of the ruling SPS. The 'recognition' side of the negotiation 'equation' is apparently a done deal. The negotiations still going on have to do with what the US has characterised as the 'road map' for the phased approach to sanctions relief."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit. Mr. Kirudja, just before the break, could I ask you to briefly describe the general situation of the closure of the border and the incident involving sightings of Yugoslav helicopters crossing the border from Serbia into Bosnia. Can you just give us the background and then we'll pick up the detail after the break.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president of -- President Milosevic at that time did take a decision, the result of which that border was closed to all except humanitarian assistance. That was -- and to monitor that the border was closed to all but humanitarian border, there was a monitoring mission that was outside the mandate of the UN. It was run by the ICFY monitors. And that situation of the closure of the border has also to be seen under Resolution 7801 of the Security Council, prohibiting military flight in the skies outside of Serbia and Montenegro. So in that context, at one date, the UN contingent, the Dutch contingent that was in Srebrenica, did notice and report the sudden appearance of helicopter flights from across the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you gives the approximate time frame you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have them right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If that's a convenient spot for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, just before the break, you were telling us about Dutch UN troops in the Srebrenica area that observed helicopters crossing the border. Did something also occur during this sighting with respect to United Nations military observers that were stationed in a radar control room in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Procedurally, before we broke, I was also asked about two other questions. Do you want me to answer them now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let's do that. The first one, I think, was the death of Mayor Obradovic. Did you have an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My notes say early July 1992. And I had a second matter that I also wanted to be clarified. The commission I was struggling to remember was called joint military commission. That was the subject of that meeting that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That joint military commission was a commission that Mr. Milosevic wanted revived after the Operation of Flash that ended up taking Sector West. That meeting in that context, after Sector West. And in that joint military commission was made up of the force commander Rupert, Mr. -- the head of the Muslim group, and the head of the Serbian VRS. In that meeting, that's when Mr. Milosevic mentioned the comment that, "Mladic is a personal friend of mine" but not so with Karadzic and Krajisnik at that point, because he regarded them as promoting the war option, that he was against. That's in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple matters of clarification. When you say "Rupert," do you mean General Rupert Smith?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say after Flash, is that the Croatian offensive that resulted in the re-taking of Sector West from Serb-controlled areas?
