utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that meeting was held in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once again back to the sighting of the helicopters. Could you please describe for us what if anything was unusual with respect to United Nations military observers at the time the sightings were made.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to those sightings, we had access to the radar room, meaning United Nations military observers in Belgrade had routine access to the military radar room for the purposes of observing Resolution 781, the no-fly around. Two or three days before the sightings, we had reports of certain unusual events leading to the military observers claiming they had no access to the room. There were complaints that they were being prevented to have access to that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who denied them access?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their counterparts. They always observed with their Serbian counterparts in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they -- their counterparts had been members of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the stated reason for members of the Yugoslav army refusing access to the UNMOs when they previously had granted them access to observe the radar screens?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only official reason I can give you is the one that was given to me ex post facto, not before. I got an explanation when I met with Ambassador Cicanovic. That is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's person in charge of relationship with UNPROFOR, and I had many dealings with him. For example, to get an explanation like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarise --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation -- the explanation was it was a misunderstanding. There were failures in the control room due to missing parts because of the sanctions against Yugoslavia. So basically, it was a misunderstanding on the part of the UN UNMOs, that they thought they were being precluded. They weren't. But this is ex post facto explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'd ask that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 12, and while that's being shown to you, did you memorialise the response of the FRY government in great detail in a report that you sent to Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in a report comprising ten pages of details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to get you to read any of that report at this stage, I just simply place it in evidence should the Chamber wish to examine more closely the examination. I ask that you now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 13. I'd ask that the second page of that document be placed on the overhead projector. The first line on the second page is "Airfield monitors in FRY." Can I draw your attention to the first paragraph of point 3 and ask you to read from that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one beginning "UNMOs..."?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNMOs have been denied access to the flight controls at Surcin airport control room. The consistent explanation has been the requirement for spare parts to repair the screen that had been assigned to the UNMOs. This flight control unit had had the parts scavenged to maintain other controls. UNMOs have been denied access to flight controls not in use and at a minimum to walk around the control room and make observations over the shoulder of the operators."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, just the paragraph that begins, number 3, "UNMOs have not been..."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNMOs have not been permitted to have an independent means of communications in their offices at the airfields or in their vehicles. Suspected violations, therefore, cannot be reported in a timely manner to permit UNPROFOR to react appropriately other than to advise UN New York belatedly. The consistent reason given is that any VHF HF communication systems used at the airfield would interfere with aircraft controlling. This is highly unlikely."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at the first page. If that could be handed to Mr. Kirudja. And was this a code cable you received from Mr. Akashi on the 13th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I now ask you that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 14. While that's being placed in front you, you've used the word "ICFY." Can you tell us what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. That was headquartered in Geneva and chaired by, at the time, by Mr. Stoltenberg on the UN side and Lord Owen on the European Union side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask that the entire exhibit be handed to Mr. Kirudja. I'd ask you to look at it and tell us whether you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask that the third page be placed -- I'm sorry. Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report that informs my headquarters that we are -- we were now exchanging reports between ICFY and us. In other words, we were going to share certain information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask that the third page of that document be placed on the overhead projector, and Mr. Kirudja, I would draw your attention to the table at the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is depicted or what does that table represent on the bottom of that report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a summary of the confiscations along the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina for the period from 4th August to 31st January, 1995, as observed by ICFY monitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this would be a record of the goods that were confiscated that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were being attempted to be brought from Yugoslavia into Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which direction, but in the border. I'm not sure which direction the goods might have been going; maybe both directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much petrol was confiscated?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on this it shows 45.368 tonnes of petrol, and 399.513 tonnes of diesel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd now ask that the last page be placed on the overhead projector. While that's being done, in your view, how effective was the border closure between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only an opinion that I couldn't back up since that responsibility was not in my hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I withdraw the question then. On the last page of that document, was there also information regarding a possible pipeline, the existence of a possible pipeline between Serbia into Bosnia under the Drina River? I draw your attention to the very last paragraph of the report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would confirm that differently in the sense that I also had one or two representations in my office from people at the other end. I forget the name, but they were also ICFY representatives, seeking our assistance in repair parts for that pipeline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit, and I would ask that the witness be shown -- or ask that the witness be shown 378, tab 15, and I'd ask that the entire exhibit be shown to Mr. Kirudja. And after you've reviewed it, Mr. Kirudja, could you tell us, do you recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a memorandum that I had sent to Mr. Akashi on 1st of March on the subject of cross-border flights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a quick look through the document, and I ask you, in this report, do you describe some reports you had of involvement of Yugoslav army troops outside the territory of Yugoslavia and in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning the entirety of the memo or a specific part of the memo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the second page of that memo.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at the second paragraph and read forward from there. See if that refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you reported, back on the 1st of March, 1995, to Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That paragraph opens with the statement: "As mentioned in previous reports, the JA -" meaning Yugoslav army - "'house' in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is caught in a wave of internal turbulence, pitting hard-liners against proponents of the 'peace option' spearheaded by Milosevic. Today word is out that written orders have been issued to all 'officers' or 'professional' soldiers in the Yugoslav army who were born on the other side of the Drina or have parents or families still living there. The order for six-month 'detachment' to either the 'RS' or 'RSK' armies. Refusal to obey the orders will result in summary dismissal. The orders seem to have been accepted without contest and do not apply to non-Serbs still in the JA even if they originate from BiH."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you go on further to talk about an anti-aircraft battery that was reported having crossed into BiH, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read that one sentence regarding that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Two days ago, two anti-aircraft infantry units the size of a brigade plus, reportedly crossed into BiH complete with their two old Soviet-made batteries of missiles of a type they call Volkov and Dina, their destination of intent not yet clear."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 26th -- or did you also report in this particular report that on the 26th of February, 1995, troops from the Yugoslav army had been seen moving toward the borders with Sector East in the vicinity of Sid not far from the Vinkovci-Mirkovci area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time that you wrote this report, would it be fair to say that Mr. Milosevic was actively involved in negotiating in the peace process?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is fair to say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions from that exhibit, or about that exhibit. I'd now ask that Mr. Kirudja be shown Prosecution Exhibit 378, tab 16. And this would be the final piece of correspondence regarding the helicopter flights I'd like to ask you about. I'd ask you to look at the entire exhibit and, after you've had a chance to review it, please tell us if you recognise it. Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a memorandum I addressed to Mr. Akashi again on the subject of the helicopter border crossings that we talked to earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask that the second page be placed on the overhead projector, and Mr. Kirudja, I would ask you to read the first sentence in the first complete paragraph of the page, the sentence beginning with, "Mr. Kertes..."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mr. Kertes, explaining that he was speaking on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia government, protested that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had not been promptly informed of the helicopter flight allegations the same day of their occurrence, and claimed that ICFY had neither the mandate nor the competence to examine such helicopter flight allegations. Of the 26 reported --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's sufficient, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this incident, had you ever been aware of Mr. Kertes's involvement in the relationship between the UNMOs and the Yugoslav army in access to the radar sites?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor was it my responsibility. This was the responsibility of the EU monitors that reported to me this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit. Thank you. Now, I want to move to a different area of inquiry. I want to ask you, did you at some point become involved in a situation or negotiations regarding UN personnel that had been taken hostage in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe in summary fashion what occurred in that incident before I ask you detailed questions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point, it was all over the news, international news, that United Nations monitors and other personnel had been taken hostage in the area within the vicinity of Sarajevo, and there occurred -- this occurred while the border had been closed, the border between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina had been closed. In that context, immediate requirement arose for the release of these hostages, first from Sarajevo itself and the commander, General Rupert Smith, and later the matter reached Belgrade, where assistance was being sought in the same exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the person that you negotiated most directly with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us his entire name? Do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Right now it doesn't come straight, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you be shown a report that you drafted, and that is Exhibit 378, tab 17. I'd ask you to review the report and tell us, do you recognise what it is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a memorandum putting on record the circumstances under which I became involved in -- on the side of Belgrade in their assistance to release the hostages through Mr. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of that report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9 June 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Stanisic's position at the time that you were negotiating with him for the release of the hostages in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that he was chief of Serbian internal -- Interior Ministry and other special security forces. Not in great detail, the title wasn't given to me in great detail, just an understanding that he was chief of -- he was chief of Serbian Interior Ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many times did you meet with him in connection with the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the exact number isn't clear to me, but at least three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were those meetings held?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time that you had meetings with him in his office, can you tell us who would have been present?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just myself and one staff member that helped me record what I was being told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Stanisic have any other members of his staff or other people from other parts of the either Serbian or federal government with him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the hostages that you were specifically negotiating? Do you recall where in Bosnia they were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, that was the subject of the negotiation. There had been a release of a certain number of personnel taken hostage. Some at that point had been released. I forget how many, but the others were not identifiable as to location or who was holding them, and that was the gist of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just as a general matter before I ask you a specific question about that report, can you describe for the Chamber when it is that you generate these reports with respect to having conducted a meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually within hours. Certainly at the end of the day or, at most, the next day. Of any matter that we were involved on, it was a requirement that you file a report for that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to the notes in your diaries, you've read a couple of passages from them. When are the -- when did you generate the diary entries with respect to --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same, and for every one of those diaries and what we have read, a report within the same day or at most 24 hours, was sent to headquarters corresponding to the subject discussed and the material details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask that the second page of that report be placed on the overhead projector. Mr. Kirudja, I want to ask you to read from paragraph number 5. If you would read that entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Stanisic proposes, if you confirm there is indeed an armed UN group in a situation as described, that he would go to the Bosnian territory while maintaining contact with our office in Belgrade, and set up a means of identifying his forces from those of the Serb captors on the ground. Simultaneously, the blocked UN group would receive coordinating orders leading to a 'cross-over' to Stanisic's forces."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus on one part of that. Where Mr. Stanisic -- where you write that Mr. Stanisic conveys to you that he will set up a means of identifying his forces, given the context of the entire conversation, did you interpret that to mean that Mr. Stanisic, after this meeting, was going to send in some of his forces into Bosnia for the specific task of locating the hostages, or did you interpret that to mean that his forces were already present in Bosnia and he would simply identify the ones most critical to the hostage situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My strong understanding is that he had in place already forces in Bosnia which he needed to contact discreetly for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. I'd ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit number 18 -- tab 18 of 378.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are -- there are no specific questions I wanted to ask you regarding this document. I want to introduce it for the sake of completeness. Is this another report of a subsequent meeting you had with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a correction on it, and it should be the one handwritten, 10 June 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for a matter of clarity, a number of the reports that you have spoken to today have underlining and certain scribbles on them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Did you do any of the underlining or any of the other writing on any of these reports?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this was originating from me, and actually, I had never seen them after I sent them until the -- this process brought them to my notice complete with those markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would just state for the record that the documents were received in this condition. These marks are not the product of anything the Office of the Prosecutor has done and I would request that the Chamber simply ignore the underlines and handwritten marks contained on the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Now, Mr. Kirudja, I would ask you, in conclusion of your testimony here, can you, based on your experience and your dealings with Mr. Milosevic and other members of the -- both the federal Yugoslav government and the Republic of Serbia government, can you describe for us what opinion, if you have any, of Mr. Milosevic's role and authority vis-a-vis other members of those governments that you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the things that struck me as interesting was Mr. Milosevic's command of detail and knowledge of matters that we sought to see him, and without this normal -- if you meet with government officials at his level, certainly he -- at the level -- summit level like his, usually there is always aides who are the keepers of the details of the issues being discussed. He struck me as very informed from policy, all the way down to detail. That was a speciality I noted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your negotiations, were you ever directed to the then sitting federal president, Mr. Zoran Lilic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never an issue. It didn't arise either from Mr. Akashi or from anybody else to request meetings with that -- on that source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to a report of the 16th of May, 1995, did you in that report express your concern to your superiors that Mr. Milosevic had too much of a solo role in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a concern, it was to draw their attention. I want to preface that all these reports were written long before this court or even the idea of this court existed. So there was a reason I wrote those reports, and that was the result to make sure that the people I was reporting to understood in greater detail the risks we learned and the things that we made our mission at risk of fail. One of those is to understand who it is they were dealing with, and therefore, in order to -- in the case of Mr. Milosevic, it was important for them to know he was very well-informed. There's no need to think of big delegations when you meet him or to request a lot of other people. It was sufficient that you met with him and he would be informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make this observation in official reports that you --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Just as an administerial matter and a way of taking stock, the Prosecution is seeking to tender all of the exhibits used with this witness, Prosecution Exhibit 378, tabs 1 through 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We admit the exhibits normally unless there is any form of objection. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no interpretation. Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear the interpretation now, not prior to this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it seems to be working now. Mr. Kirudja, when you arrived in Krajina, the Sector North, and the entire area, Krajina, Croatia, Bosnia, everywhere you moved around, you came across a situation there, and was it your impression that the Yugoslav People's Army and other authorities extended full cooperation and support to you in what you considered to be your task and assignment there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Mr. Milosevic. It is correct that the Yugoslav national army did extend, as I testified earlier, what I considered full cooperation to the UN mission, at least in the early stages of its deployment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So may we then take it that with respect to logistical support, the army and the authorities of Yugoslavia demonstrated towards you their readiness to fully cooperate and see that your mission was a success and fulfilled its assignment? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I stress there was an issue of cooperation as we started our deployment. There were other details of my testimony that point to changes thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to those changes and then I should like to ask you for some additional explanations in that regard, but as a conscientious representative of the United Nations with the mandate you were given, I assume that you did not omit to become acquainted, once you arrived in Yugoslavia, with the most important provisions of the constitution of Yugoslavia. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are partly right. I was, of course, obligated to understand the mandate of the mission, as we spoke earlier, the Vance Plan being a component of that, plus the subsequent resolutions of the UN that mandated that. With regard to the constitution of Yugoslavia, I regrettably say I can't say I am familiar with that constitution, nor was I required really to become familiar with its contents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you acquainted at least with some of the principles, such as the principle mirrored in the constitution which speaks about the inalienable right and duty of the peoples and nationalities of Yugoslavia, the citizens of Yugoslavia, to protect and defend their independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, in one of the meetings that we had with you, if you recall over lunch at the break, I had the pleasure of having you explain me a certain point on that constitution that I still treasure to this day, because you did give me a very impassioned explanation. If you recall, I had asked you to clarify for me an issue that had become very constant claim by the Serbs who were in Sector North and elsewhere wherein they kept reminding me of a speech given by Mr. Tudjman on one Christmas not long after the declaration of independence that stated that Croatia was a state of Croats, and that, they said to us at the UN, how do you expect us to live in a state where the president tells us it's the state of Croats? So, Mr. Milosevic, I did ask you to explain to me is the constitution of Yugoslavia different? Does it speak of Yugoslavia -- Serbia as a state of Serbs? And I was pleasantly surprised of your explanation, which you might remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, because it was the constitution of Serbia which was enacted in 1990, and Article 1 of that constitution states that the Serbs -- that the state of Serbia is a state of all its citizens.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did explain to me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you know, Mr. Kirudja, during the time you spent on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and later on in these past ten years - I assume you'll be able to confirm that - nowhere on the territory of Serbia and the new Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was formed on the 28th of April, 1992, did you have any ethnic conflicts or acts of discrimination on the part of citizens of other ethnic groups or, rather, 28 nationalities, 28 ethnic groups live in Serbia, and there were no acts of discrimination which you were able to point your finger to or to, indeed, witness. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if I heard you correctly, you referred to the last ten years. Mr. Milosevic, the testimony I give here is ten years ago, going back to 1992. Part of that testimony clearly indicates I did leave, I left my role at the UN since then. So I couldn't, obviously, testify for the time I was away. So in order to answer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put myself right. I wasn't thinking over the past ten years, i was thinking of the past 12 years or 13 years or throughout the time, let's say from 1989 onwards, up to the year 2000. And all these years encompass the period of your sojourn in Yugoslavia. So I used the term ten years, I said ten years more or less symbolically, to symbolise a decade, but of course, starting out from the first day of your presence there and then throughout your stay, that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Of course, if you ask me for the time I was there, unfortunately, much of the testimony you heard today is contrary to that because we are testifying about the events that occurred that point to a concerted effort, at least in the area that I knew, of Serb authorities to force Muslims out. At least in the area that I testified to. So generally, your statement would, of course, not be correct, at least in those cases that I testified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not about Bosnia, Krajina, Croatia, but about Serbia, Serbia and Montenegro or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your apologies. I didn't understand that specific reference. In that case, my answer would be not to my knowledge in those particular areas of what constitutes Serbia and Montenegro, I wouldn't have any evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I hope, Mr. Kirudja, that you could have heard just evidence to the contrary, that is to say of a highly tolerant atmosphere and a lot of care and attention on the part of the authorities to see that there was no discrimination.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me my personal impression?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer you in the positive in the sense that my presence in Serbia, I had a complete feel of personal security, no hostility that were ever directed to me, and I did visit wide areas of Serbia in all kinds of circumstances. You are right. I personally didn't feel any discrimination directed to me. Now, I say that. If you ask me elsewhere, outside, I did elsewhere, but not in that area that you specifically refer to, Serbia and Montenegro, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. You know that during that time I was president of Serbia, so I'm asking you about the territory which I considered myself to be responsible for.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kirudja, as you were speaking here and giving examples and speaking in detail about these examples - we'll come to that later on- but you mentioned refugees, and do you know that we in Serbia at one point had as many as 1 million refugees? Are you aware of that? Coming in from different parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was the recipient of a number of statements about the presence of refugees in Serbia, and your -- at that time people who were under you in the humanitarian did make presentations to us about the presence of refugees in Serbia and Montenegro. However, at no time did I hear or retain a figure in millions. I don't know what the figure was, simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at one particular point the figure had reached that particular number. But when you were in Yugoslavia yourself, do you happen to recall, for example, the piece of information according to which in Serbia alone there was -- let's take this concrete example: 70.000 Muslim refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, to quote an example, and from the territories engulfed by war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to authenticate the figure of 70.000 or did I hear it? Is that the specific question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear about that figure?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did hear there were a lot of refugees of all kinds, and I did meet even Muslims in Serbia. So the fact that there were refugees that were Muslim in Serbia, yes, I can say that I met some. How many there were, the exact numbers, that I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This wasn't your responsibility or duty to deal with things of that kind, but these Muslim refugees that you happened to meet in Serbia that you mentioned, did they complain at all of the treatment they were being given in Serbia which would discriminate against them in any way? So they had arrived in Serbia to take refuge from the war that was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, hadn't they? Now, did they live there as citizens on a footing of equality with everybody else, without any special treatment, regime, or any kind of discrimination? Did they live Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like any other citizen, like all the other citizens, in fact?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I could testify to that that one of my interpreters was a Muslim that was relocated from Serbian -- from Bihac and continued to work peacefully in Belgrade. So at least even directly in my front office, I had an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'm happy to hear that. But let's go back to the constitution for a moment. Did you know that the defence of the territorial integrity of the country was one of the constitutionally based foremost tasks of the armed forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't really have an occasion to delve into that kind of detail. I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to clear up one particular point, Mr. Kirudja. In your statement where you speak about the 21st of April, 1992, it says, among others, "Among the representatives of the local authorities --" and I'm quoting you on that -- "who came to us in the UN were Colonel Slobodan Tarbuk, the local commander of what started to be called the forces of Territorial Defence," and in brackets you have "TO." So the members of the TO decided to take that name, to be called in that way because they wished to differentiate themselves from the JNA, which was expected, in keeping with the UN mandate, to withdraw from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The statement is in excess of 60 pages. It would be very helpful if Mr. Milosevic could provide at least a ballpark reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has the witness got a copy? Do you have a copy, Mr. Kirudja, of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kirudja will, I'm sure, remember that passage, but that's not what I'm basing my question on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's a statement of 60 pages. Let the witness have it. Which page is it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, I don't mind giving the witness a chance to look at all of this. I'm quoting from his passage about the 21st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question relates to the following, Mr. Kirudja: Is it clear to you--

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... page 6, Your Honour--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must be entitled to have the page. So when you quote the statement and the witness has got it, let's have the page number so he can follow. We've got this. Page 6, yes. At some stage the Chamber may need copies but for the moment we will go on without.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, they do not have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, or rather, did you know at the time, Mr. Kirudja, that the Territorial Defence was not something that was created then and there as a substitute in any way for the Yugoslav People's Army? It was something that had existed beforehand. It was part of the armed forces pursuant to the constitution, the type of organisation formed at local level throughout the territory of the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the meeting you refer to is on 21st of April, as you pointed out. You may note that it was the first time the force commander had come into the sector and the local authorities who were meeting him and making a presentation to that. Conclusion that is implicit in that meeting is that the terms of the Vance Plan had already been placed in motion. The terms of the Vance Plan that I take it that you are also very familiar with. Under those terms, you must also conclude, the issue to Territorial Defence force was alien to that force, was actually proscribed. There were not to be any forces like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about something else. I don't know whether we understand each other. It's not that the Territorial Defence was formed as a substitute for the JNA. It had existed previously as a form of direct defence involvement on the part of the citizens throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So it existed far before the conflicts broke out. It existed as part of the defence and protection system of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to speak authoritatively, obviously, on what was there before we arrived in a different context and a different purpose. If you say so, Mr. Milosevic, I wouldn't have a way of disputing the point about things which were in the former Yugoslavia before we came in, before the mandate was framed. Of course I wouldn't be able to know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I wish to do is to challenge something, a misunderstanding probably on your part, according to which you concluded, as far as I was able to gather, that the Territorial Defence was in fact established then as a substitute for the JNA. And all I'm saying is it existed much earlier on and was, in fact, and I'd like -- focused upon and mirrored in the Yugoslav constitution, because the constitution stipulates in Article 240.2 of the constitution, the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia make up a whole and are composed of the Yugoslav People's Army as a joint armed force of all the peoples and nationalities, et cetera, and is also composed of the Territorial Defence as the broadest form of the organisation for the defence forces. Therefore, the Territorial Defence - and this is what I want to ask you whether you understand - was not formed as a substitute for the army but it was in existence as part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, and this was provided for by the constitution at the time when Yugoslavia was united, one country, and that's when it was in existence. So are you aware of that fact? It was the existing part of the armed forces. So it wasn't established as a reaction to the Vance Plan. That's what I want to make clear.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will return, may it please the Court, to my statement that the TDF, and my use of that term was in the context of the attempt to demobilise the existing forces as required in the Vance Plan, and that demobilisation was not qualified. It was supposed to be total. There shall be no armed forces with big weapons except police for the purposes of law and order. As soon as we sought to make that a reality, then cropped the issue of Territorial Defence forces and given various reasons the Serbs give us, like defence of their borders from Croat infiltrators. That is the context in which this explanation is given. I just re-emphasise that. Explanation about the existence of the concept of Territorial Defence force in the constitution of Yugoslavia, as Mr. Milosevic explained, may or may not be true. I couldn't speak to that. I was speaking in the exact context I described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that Croatia, in 1991, started to effect a secession from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my understanding that by the time we arrived, there were recognised by the UN the states of Croatia and other constituents of Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, when we arrived. It is also my understanding that within the State of Croatia -- or, rather, it's not an understanding, it's self-evident, there had been an area carved out of that Croatia where our mission was to help resolve those disputed territories. When or under what circumstances Croatia seceded from the former Yugoslavia in 1991 I am, unfortunately, not conversant with the details of that in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were -- you didn't deal with that, but I'm sure you know that it was emphasised that it was the function of the Vance Plan to achieve peace and to ensure the safety and security of citizens on territories in which there had been conflict. And another important characteristic of it was that the presence of the United Nations forces in areas under UN protection does not -- does not mean that a political solution is implied but that a political solution should be sought through political means. Isn't that so? And if you just shake your head, this cannot be recorded. So may we have an audible answer from you, please.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for you to stop, and I will of course give you an audible answer. Pretty much everything you have said, with one major difference, if I heard you correctly, where you mentioned that the United Nations' responsibility for maintaining law and order while a political solution was being sought. Mr. Milosevic, you're sure that is not quite correct. The law and order was to be kept by local police and the mayors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish so that he can give his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. So the law and order, a very crucial part, was left in the local hands, and that was -- the only role the UN had was to monitor that that function was properly executed. Now, as you recall one of my testimonies here, I did allude to that turning into a big loophole in terms of the UN being unable to fulfil that part of the resolution responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you mean the monitoring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not the monitoring. The failure for -- in other words, I did testify that because the Serbs transformed the forces that were essentially military forces into the semblance of a police force for both in strength beyond the requirement of the Vance Plan as well in terms of numbers, as well as in weapons, they became what they called the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina for the purposes of pursuing goals such as independence for that area. So if the UN had the responsibility for maintaining law and order, then its own forces, the forces of the UN that were there, would have come in different composition and in different numbers. They had come only to observe maintenance of law and order at the hands of the local police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But we are talking about UN protected areas, not zones that are monitored by the UN, but they are protected by the UN. We are talking about those areas. So I assume that it is legitimate to ask whether the United Nations protected these areas and the population in them. But we'll come to that. Tell me, Mr. Kirudja, you came for the Vance Plan, and I assume that you familiarised yourself with the events that preceded the adoption of the Vance Plan, that you familiarised yourself with the causes that led to the conflict or, rather, the reasons why the conflict broke out. And after that, the Vance Plan was adopted, and the peacekeeping forces were deployed, or, rather, the UN Protective Forces were deployed. That was the name. So do you know that the first serious incidents in Krajina took place when the Croat authorities, in the autumn of 1990, started taking away the weapons of the local police and the Territorial Defence in the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we need to consider this: The relevance to the witness's evidence. These were events before the witness came on the scene. He, therefore, can't speak directly about them, and really to rehearse these events with him is not going to take the case any further forward. You can ask him about events, of course, after he arrived, but there's little point in asking him about events before then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I asked Mr. Kirudja, since he had come to carry out an important task, whether he was familiar with what had preceded the Vance Plan and what the reasons were for the adoption of the Vance Plan to begin with, and was he aware of what the problems were beforehand. If there is a problem, then I will drop it, but does he know how the hostilities actually came to exist, that's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to be his state of mind, unless you can show its relevance, is not going to take us any further forward.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kirudja, that Serbs in Krajina did not recognise the secession of Croatia since it was contrary to the constitution of Yugoslavia, the constitution that was then valid in Yugoslavia, as well as contrary to international law? Therefore, there would be a violent degradation in the rights that they enjoyed on a footing of equality with other citizens in the Republic of Croatia and in Yugoslavia as a whole. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of that question to the witness's evidence? I know it's your case, which you've put often enough, but it seems to me not to be relevant to the witness's evidence, whether Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he knew or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance, Mr. May, is in the undoubtedly undeniable right of the Serb people which -- and that is a right that cannot be taken away from any people. That is the right to self-defence. The relevance lies in the following: That we should establish that the Serb people were indeed threatened in that territory and that exercising their right to self-defence, they had many things happening that were related to that right, and I'm asking the witness, who was there at the time when all these events took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That is an issue which we, no doubt, are going to have to determine, because as we've heard before, that is, as I've said before, it is your case that this was a matter of the local Serbs defending themselves. Now, the witness's view about that, with all respect to him, is totally irrelevant, and rehearsing what happened before he came, as I've said, is not going to advance the case. It's just taking up time unnecessarily. You can do it with other witnesses who deal with that period. What, if I may say, you should concentrate on is the witness's evidence in relation to his time when he was in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'm going to skip a few questions then. Irrespective of your efforts, these issues cannot be sidestepped. But anyway, I shall be quite precise with regard to the questions put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That kind of comment is wholly unnecessary and wholly untrue. These are issues which you have raised, and they will be dealt with in due course, and you must understand that. But meanwhile, what we're discussing is the relevance to this witness's evidence. Now, would you concentrate, in cross-examination, on relevant matter. That's all you're being told to do. Now, let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR command, was it well-informed about the situation in the field?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. At the very beginning, we of course had to keep an open mind and learn as we got to know what was on the ground. So our knowledge - and I speak now collectively since you put it as UNPROFOR - we did learn a lot before and even more during the time we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. I'm referring to the period that you spent there. So what you say now, does that mean that, not taking into account individual incidents, truly some individual incidents that could have gone by unnoticed irrespective of your presence in the field, but can we establish that not a single more significant event or process could not go unnoticed by members of UNPROFOR? I mean, by your personnel, by other members of UNPROFOR, et cetera. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, it's a little more complicated for me to take a blanket situation that everything was noticed by us. We noticed what we have talked about. I wouldn't be surprised if somebody said there was an event XYZ and I didn't notice it. Such is life. We didn't know everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about more significant events, processes, happenings. So can we assume that more significant events could not go by unnoticed or unregistered by your mission and by UNPROFOR, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct. Much of my testimony has to do with those events we considered were significant. Everything? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Does that mean that with regard to all these major events, all these more significant events or, rather, regarding everything that you learned about, did your vertical chain have to be informed accordingly? That is to say, all the people who headed your organisation, UNPROFOR, et cetera. You didn't keep anything to yourself, did you? Everything that you found out on the ground was vertically sent up to the very top, to General Nambiar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, thank you for giving me that question. A little earlier I did say we went every mile to report what we thought was significant to our headquarters, even inclusive of testimony here, at one point I get the UN telling me, "Don't do this. You are getting too involved." So it wasn't like we were holding back anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sent everything up. You reported on everything; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of what I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said in several sections that you met with General Nambiar. Tell me, what were your impressions of him? Was this a good, conscientious, able, professional soldier, an honourable man, in every conceivable respect a person who was up to the job that he had?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pleased to say yes, I consider him in the category of that, and I got to know him well, and I can say yes, he was a professional, conscientious man who was well-suited for the job he took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read out to you his statement since he spoke about events that took place in Yugoslavia. At that time, he was director of an institution called United Services Institution of India, and he says that he and his people, while he was in Yugoslavia, that is to say both he and you and everybody else who made up this mission that consisted of several thousands of people, there is quotation: "[In English] [previous translation continues...] witness any genocide beyond killings and massacres on all sides that are typical of such conflict conditions."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read me a statement of General Nambiar. I haven't seen it. If you say it was his statement, the only thing I can say is it is a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you doubt that this is his statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know what it is. I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I don't hold it against you, the fact that you did not see it. It is not your duty to follow his statements. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How could he have seen it? Mr. Groome, is this something which you disclosed to the Defence, one of your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's new to me, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. There's even less reason that you should have seen it. All right. We'll accept for the moment that it's a statement which you have from the general. I suppose what you can ask the witness is that, having heard that statement, is there any comment that you would like to make about it or not? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- facilitate matters. Can I just say something? In order to make it easier for Mr. Kirudja, I'm going to go on with my questions, and during the break, which is coming up, as far as I can see on the clock, I'm going to give your technical booth a tape with this statement of General Nambiar's, and after that, Mr. Kirudja, if he wishes to, may comment on it. That is certainly within his rights. So let's not waste any time now regarding a possible explanation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, he says that violence was on all sides in the situation of that type of conflict. Do you agree, Mr. Kirudja, that when there is that kind of a civil war, an ethnic conflict, that the only thing that can be done is to bring the conflict to a stop, that no small corrections can be made through any partial remedies. The only solution is bringing the conflict to an end and going back to political means. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a lengthy question and there are several parts to it. The part that I zero on is the issue of violence which you referred to as existing. That is something I can say, yes, we did see violence in -- from the three groups, but it wasn't of equal magnitude or weight. Second -- in terms of numbers involved, in terms of repercussions, in terms of impact; there were by no means equal. Secondly, if you ask me whether peaceful solution was the way out, obviously we would agree with you, and we did in the meetings we met with you, because such was the UN nature there is to find a peaceful solution. It goes without saying that is something we would have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your experience throughout your stay there, was there anything that official Serbia did and that I personally did, was anything going outside the framework of that general objective, to attain peace and a peaceful solution? Do you know of anything that was not done in that direction?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid the question is of such broad nature that I could only respond to you partially. My testimony here contains what we heard from you, and towards the end of the questioning, you heard me repeat honestly and bluntly that was your preference, that there be a peaceful solution. As regards to anything and everything that happened that may have been contrary to that policy, with due respect, I cannot answer that because I wasn't privy to everything that would be in that domain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. You are talking about what you know. Now, the fact the commander of UNPROFOR says that this is not genocide and that he bears in mind the high quality monitoring system that you established and the system of reporting from the area of Krajina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, can that be considered as a reliable statement, an authentic statement in respect of what I've been asking you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness cannot comment on that. For one thing, genocide is a technical term and one of the issues which we're going to have to determine in this case as the indictment in Bosnia contains such an allegation. Now, you said you were going to play a tape afterwards. It's now time for the adjournment, so we'll take it now, and perhaps you can set the tape up to be played in the next session. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have a tape. On the tape we don't have this particular statement, but he made an identical statement in India in 2001 -- 2001 was when he -- too was when he made this particular statement. He was speaking at the university and made the statement in front of students there, and you'll see on it on the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Question: [No interpretation] "General Nambiar: [Indiscernible] Bosnia-Herzegovina was one of my responsibilities. So these 28.000 troops were spread out in all the parts of the former Yugoslavia except Slovenia. And to answer your question very directly, the other part of your question, as far as commander -- I was commander of UNPROFOR, none of my troops ever gave me any reports of genocide because they were not [indiscernible] genocide. There were allegations by other people from [indiscernible] area, but my troops were not participating in genocide. They never reported any such things to me, and therefore I never reported any -- [indiscernible]."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this General Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you now comment this statement of his?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to make a brief observation. A statement is contained in that tape where General Nambiar is saying, if I understood him correctly, "None of my forces reported to me incidents of genocide." I believe that was the word. General Nambiar, I said earlier, had a wonderful sense of propriety, integrity, and being extremely careful and precise with his words. Notice he said, "None of my forces." I want to put on record that there is a memo that I read out here listing out a number of places where I used the word, "We were told there are concentration camps," starting with Keraterm and ending, I believe, the Omarska or somewhere. Several number of places. I recall clearly when General Nambiar got a hold of that copy. He was the only one in my headquarters - not my boss Cedric, not anybody else- who called me about it. He was very concerned about whether this was true. And being a gentleman he was, and I underscore he was very polite and nice, we remained in touch even after he left UNPROFOR, directly with me. He sought to caution me over the use of the word "concentration camp" that appears in the memo, and true to his caution, he called me, "Charles, did you really say this is so?" I said, "Yes. This was being reported. But if you don't like --" I remember that conversation -- "concentration camp, what would you like to call them?" I asked him, and he said, "Maybe detention camps." I said, "No, the situation was worse on that." And as the photographs came later, you all recall subsequently, there are photographs coming from that area, we weren't exaggerating rating it. Now, notice that statement now, he said, "None of my forces." I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wasn't one of his forces. So he may be accurate in what he said, but I wasn't one of his forces, and I certainly didn't report to him. He called me back about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but without a doubt he was informed of all the reports, including your own reports, the reports you sent.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My point was that he might be correct technically to say none of his forces but factually not complete because he didn't regard me. I certainly was not one of his forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. In your statement, you state the following: "Up until the beginning of April, many countries, including the European Union, recognised the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this speeded up the deterioration of the situation that we noted in Bosnia and had a great influence on our work in Sector North." Now, could you explain to us this negative effect that the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina had, in fact?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have the page number again? Do you have the page number you quoted me from, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I do not, but I assume you can recognise your position.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise the paragraph. It would just be more exact if you gave me the quote source itself. Nevertheless, since I recognise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, let's find this. If you're going to cross-examine witnesses on statements, they need to be referred to the particular paragraph, because it's only fair that they should have that in front of them when they answer so they have the context. What we'll do, Mr. Milosevic, is we'll go on, and we'll get this paragraph found, but let's not waste any more time at this stage on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you happen to know, Mr. Kirudja, that before the beginning of the war in Bosnia - on the 17th of March, 1992, in fact - the leaders of the three national communities in Bosnia signed a declaration on the principles for the new constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was what was known as the Cutilheiro plan, according to which Bosnia would be one single state within its present borders with three constituent national units or ethnic groups, and that plan could have preserved peace. However, Izetbegovic, following suggestions from the then ambassador of the United States of America to Yugoslavia, Warren Zimmermann, withdrew his signature. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the term Cutilheiro rings a bell but no more than that, neither the date when it was dated. I do not have recollections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't remember the event and the facts that I've just mentioned linked to the plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it being something that we were involved on or sufficient for me to know its content.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall read out what in April 1999 General Nambiar said in his capacity as head of the -- this institution, the Indian institution that I quoted a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection. The witness has stated he has no recollection, nothing to offer the Chamber on this. This appears to be an attempt to have Nambiar's views on it put in through this witness, which is inappropriate. Certainly the Prosecution, if Mr. Milosevic seeks to call Mr. Nambiar, the Prosecution wouldn't object to it. If Mr. Milosevic wants to supply us with copies of these statements, we will review them, and maybe by stipulation introduce the statements of Nambiar, but I think using this witness to bring these statements in is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness -- the accused can ask what is in the statement, provided it's relevant, and the witness can deal with it. He can put the statement to the witness. He's entitled to do that provided, as I say, it's relevant, and the witness can answer. Of course, the fact that a statement is put to a witness, as we have said before, does not make it evidence. Now, Mr. Milosevic, is this about the Cutilheiro plan and -- what you've been just asking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It relates to peace in Bosnia, the conclusion of peace in Bosnia, and the obstacles to it, and we felt it in particular, those of us who wanted to have peace achieved, Mr. May. And I don't want to insist upon the fact that Mr. Kirudja should respond to the question if he does not wish to do so. All I would like to have are his comments in view of the fact that he was the official UN representative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. We will have -- we will have the quotation. We will hear whether Mr. Kirudja can deal with it. Let us hear the beginning of it anyway, of what you want to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the quotation, it's fairly brief. I'm just going to ask him to answer and tell us whether this coincides with what he saw. This is General Nambiar's statement, and he says: "It is ironic that the Dayton Agreement of Bosnia was not fundamentally different from the Lisbon plan drawn by Portuguese Foreign Minister Cutilheiro and British representative Lord Carrington, [In English] to which all three sides had agreed before any killings had taken place -- before any killings had taken place or even the Vance-Owen Plan which Karadzic was willing to sign. One of the main problems was that there was unwillingness on the part of the American administration to consider Serbs had legitimate grievance --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we're getting beyond the scope of this witness's evidence. One quotation has been put to you, which was this, that the Dayton Agreement was not fundamentally different from the Cutilheiro plan and the Carrington Plan. Again, do you feel you can comment on that usefully, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think only to place it in context on why I couldn't comment on it, and that is that the Cutilheiro-Carrington reference is to the heads of ICFY. Prior to the mission being instituted in former Yugoslavia and the Dayton agreement which he is comparing it to is well after my departure from that area. So both events place me outside of direct knowledge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were next going to be asked about the American administration and their position about the Serbs. Is that something you could comment at all on or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't, because the context is not there for me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask Mr. Kirudja this: Do you remember when he says, "In connection with that --" as General Nambiar says -- "I recall State Department official George --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We've ruled that the witness cannot deal with that. Now, unless it's something directly related to him, he cannot deal with the American administration. It's not for him to answer about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this doesn't only relate to that issue. General Nambiar says that as George Kenney had this same position and attitude, he said, "I offered to give him an escort and to go see for himself that --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who did he offer? Who offered to give who an escort?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Satish Nambiar offered the diplomat George Kenney to give Kenney an escort to go and see for himself what he was claiming, or some of what he was claiming. And he goes on to say: "He accepted my offer, and thereafter he made a radical turnaround."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I'm going to rule against this. It's not something the witness can deal with. If you want to call General Nambiar, you can, in due course in your case, but you can't ask this witness about something he can't deal with. It's neither fair to him nor is it proper use of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have absolutely no intention of not being fair towards Mr. Kirudja. I thought he was in a position to comment on these issues. But if you consider he is not, then we needn't pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you consider that recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina speeded up the deterioration of the situation in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified here that when the mission UNPROFOR was set up, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a relatively peaceful place, completely peaceful when we arrived there, to the extent that the mission structure was done recognising this and hoping the peaceful situation would continue to the extent that the headquarters of the mission was supposed to be Sarajevo, and we had two battalions, logistic battalions, based in Banja Luka. That estimation by the UN turned out to be incorrect, and in the time line mentioned by Mr. Milosevic is the only association I can see. Not cost relationship, just time line association. That soon after that recognition about the time we were there, we watched the entire Bosnia get involved in a conflagration and the headquarters of the UNPROFOR was moved out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that some highly respected politicians, such as Francois Mitterrand or Lord Peter Carrington, and some others too, claimed that the early recognition of Croatia was a mistake too and that it made the peace process impossible? Are you aware of that in view of the fact that these were things that you dealt with at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for this witness who is -- who was an official at the UN at the time, to comment on what either President Mitterrand or Lord Carrington said. Now, if you want to call evidence about that, as I say, you can do so. But not only is it not fair to this witness, his views about it, with respect, are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May, fine. Then I'll go back to some very specific and concrete questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified, and I saw some statements to that effect in your statement -- I'm very happy, actually, to see that -- we're talking about Lazarevic. Yesterday you mentioned Lazarevic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm very happy to see that you confirm what I had thought too, that Lazarevic was a rogue. That was your conclusion, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I didn't use the word "rogue," if you recall, but I did testify to my being extremely cautious and wary of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he did a lot of harm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That he organised the arrest of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he probably did so for his own personal gain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that was not his evidence. Mr. Lazarevic's evidence was that he was acting under instructions and with a purpose to instruct. So to that extent, it must be said that this witness's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information, evidence, rather, confirms what Mr. Lazarevic said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think, Mr. May, quite the reverse is true. The testimony of this witness proves that Lazarevic did a lot of harm and that Lazarevic misled his own compatriots as well, because if he translates a conversation wrongly, for example, between Mr. Spanovic and Mr. Kirudja, then he's not doing a service to his side let alone to Mr. Kirudja's side itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be a matter for us to judge in due course, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, "During the mission, I learnt not to accept any information he gave me without checking it out, and that from independent sources." So you concluded that he was prone to lie.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- he gave me a distinct feeling that I was being hassled by him.
