utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be of assistance. This is on page 5 of the English version of the statement given by Mr. Kirudja to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the officials in Krajina, then, tell you that behind this rigged arrest of Mrs. Indira Kulenovic, that behind it all was Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the meeting following immediately my initial complaint meeting with Mr. Mile Paspalj, Mr. Toso Paic hurriedly came to a second meeting where he sought to put a distance between what my complaints were and explaining that it was caused by Lazarevic, if that's what you mean. But I didn't say I believed completely what he said. I just said that's what he told me. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And did I understand you correctly when explaining his position? As far as I understood it, he was an interpreter and Bulat was the liaison officer. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I have just been claiming, that he was an ordinary interpreter, and he said that he was a liaison officer, whereas Bulat was the liaison officer and he was the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction, Mr. Milosevic: Bulat was not the liaison officer. Bulat was the boss. Bulat was the commander. Lazarevic was the liaison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, did you get the idea that when he said Lazarevic did it, we had reason to believe he wasn't alone on that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I consider that probably for his own gain he did what he did. Perhaps he wanted to take up the job of this interpreter, replace him. I don't know what your conclusions are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to have regard to what the evidence was, and really, it's not for this witness. I mean, Mr. Lazarevic's evidence was that this was a deliberate plan to obstruct. He was an agent of KOS. He was part of the military intelligence and he was put in that position as liaison officer in order to obstruct the UN and other missions, and that's what he set about doing. But you can ask the witness, I suppose, this: Was there anything which Mr. Lazarevic said or anything from the circumstances which enabled you to understand why he was doing this, what his motives were? Was there any suggestion that he was doing it for personal gain or advancement or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were indications to me that whatever he was doing had those components in it, both personal and official. Both components were in it. On the personal side, it was the part I mentioned to you how I met him, how he presented himself and comes through as a hustler, trying to gain a role for himself. That's on the personal side. On the effects of interference with our work, with the evidence of the arrest of the interpreter, with the misinterpretation in the meeting in which Colonel Spanovic was there, that could not have been personal, because we did tell Bulat about it, we did tell Toso Paic, as the record shows. Djuro Skaljac executed the attempt at arrest. If they differed with him, they would have dismissed him quickly and immediately. They did the contrary; Bulat insisted he interpreted him, even after we told him so, and we told Bulat, in that case, when you speak, let Lazarevic interpret you. When we speak, when any of us speaks, somebody else will interpret. That was not personal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short while ago, you said, Mr. May, that Lazarevic worked for the KOS. The only correct thing to say is that that was his assertion. When a true officer of the service, an ethnic Muslim, testified afterwards, you managed to find out that when Lazarevic claimed to have been a member of KOS, there was no KOS. There was a security service within the army, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was KOG. We can debate all this in due course, but let's not waste any time about it with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say about Lazarevic, the following. I'm quoting you now. This is the portion that the amicus referred to. You said that: "A day or two later, I remember that after he announced his retirement, he went to Bihac to convey a message to him from the Kordun command which may have been conveyed by Lazarevic. And also there was a warning there if he were to set foot in Kordun. I felt duty-bound to relay that message because I felt that this threat was not in vain. He appreciated the warning." So although -- so it was not only that he threatened your interpreter and said that your interpreter would be arrested but he also threatened a JNA general; is that right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction, Mr. Milosevic. He conveyed not his idea that General Spiro Nikovic, who had been retired from command a day or so earlier, would be arrested if he set foot in the territory of Kordun. He wasn't. He was a liaison officer, and my understanding was that he was communicating to me, an official, something backed by his superiors. He wasn't saying, "I'm going to arrest him myself."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you say that when you first saw him, now I'm quoting you: "It is already then that I got the impression that he's the type of person who could be a good mercenary." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Kirudja, this is page 13, paragraph 1, of the English version that you have. So it is page 13 -- page 13, paragraph 1. In the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, can this also mean, since you had the impression that he could be a good mercenary, that Lazarevic, while lying to you and to the local Serb authorities and with this kind of meddling, he was actually working for a third party, not for the local Serb authorities or for UNPROFOR? Do you reject that possibility altogether or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My exact language in the English language includes the quote: "He was the stuff of which would-be mercenaries are made." That is not to say he was a mercenary, it is to say he exhibited all the qualities. In other words, somebody who did things for hire by somebody else. That's all it meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So am I right -- I mean, I'm not going to quote everything you said here because you devoted a large portion of this to Lazarevic, because you say: "After awhile, I found out from our interpreters that he interprets differently from what the speakers actually said, that he allegedly interpreted for us," et cetera, and so on and so forth. There are two pages in your statement that have to do with Lazarevic. Now, my question is: Am I right if I, on the basis of what you said, and both what I quoted from your statement and what you know yourself that you said in your statement, if one could conclude, since he could be a good mercenary is not someone who could really be respected? He is a person who is prone to lying, cheating, and you even testified to that if you say that he misinterpreted what was being said. Can one conclude that Lazarevic is a person with low moral qualities, a person that is not trustworthy?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long statement and there are many parts to it. Before I answer that, look at the date of this testimony. It is 29 September 1999, long before, if I understand correctly, the reference to testimony by Mr. Lazarevic was ever come. I was unaware of that. So what I said at this time was what I knew directly, without reference to whatever testimony you are discussing that Lazarevic gave. The conclusion you're asking me to make, you can make that if you so wish. My point here was to register the very fact that I regarded him as an unstabilising factor in the sector, a misleading factor in the sector, and someone who was quite capable of doing somebody else's bidding. That's what the reference to "would-be mercenaries" is intended to. I didn't know exactly who it was he was doing things for, I just referred to clear signs he was acting that way and that I treated him that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I asked you whether one may conclude then that Lazarevic is then a person who is of low moral fibre and who cannot be trusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's not for the witness to say that. He's given his evidence about how he found Lazarevic and that's as far as he can take it. Whether we accept or don't accept what the witness says and what Lazarevic said, that's going to be a matter for us, and you can address us on it, but you cannot take the witness's evidence any further than he already has. He's told us what happened. He's told us his opinion. Now, there's no point repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. Kirudja devotes a considerable part of your -- of his statement to him. I believe that there is not a single individual to whom he devoted more attention, and therefore, we can hear his opinion now. Perhaps he can change it after his testimony, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has given his opinion as far as he can, and his opinion is only based on what his experience of what Mr. Lazarevic did and said during the time that they were in Sector North together. Now, he's given his answer to your question about his character, Lazarevic's character. He said that he regarded him as a destabilising and misleading factor, capable of doing anybody's bidding. But whose bidding it was, he didn't know. It will be a matter for us to decide that. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we are now going to deal with this witness of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the Krajina Serbs justified the keeping of part of the armed forces in contravention of the Vance Plan and in contravention of the will of official Belgrade. You say the local Serbs justified the fact that these armed forces were being detained by the so-called inability of UNPROFOR to protect the borders of the RSK from the Croatian army on the north and the Muslim forces along the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said that you got a similar explanation from Paspalj on the 13th of May, 1992, and you said that Paspalj said that the RSK cannot be fully demilitarised because the UN is not sufficiently prepared to protect the population from a possible attack. You said the protection of the local population can only be guaranteed if UNPROFOR brings in more troops. Now, my question is the following: These objections of the Krajina Serbs, were they correct altogether? Was UNPROFOR truly not in a position to prevent them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question contains paraphrasing of a good part of my testimony. Much of that paraphrasing is correct. Some of it is a little different from the statement itself. However, in general, the bottom question is your -- are these objections of the Krajina Serbs correct altogether? I think that's the bottom line of your question. My answer to that is to refer to elsewhere in the testimony where it is stated that the Serbs failed to execute the Vance Plan and used part of it as a loophole to defeat it, to defeat the Vance Plan. Yes, you're correct that the UN forces on the ground, I have stated here, were not designed to do the protecting that you referred to. They were only designed to let the Vance Plan work with the local control and maintain the peace while a solution was being found elsewhere in the context of the ICFY. So your long question cannot be reduced to an answer of yes or no that the Serbs were correct altogether in making that. It had to be broken in part and responded, each one of them, and if you do that, you end up back in my testimony paragraph by paragraph, which is there, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. self-evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement - let's be more precise - you mentioned some of the attacks of the Croat forces against the UN protected area, Maslenica Most, Medecki Jep [phoen], et cetera. Can you recall all the large-scale actions of the Croat forces against the population there and against Krajina or, rather, the UN protected area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. In general, I can recall because there were major events that occurred in the sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that the UN forces during those attacks did not protect the Krajina Serbs who were ultimately ethnically cleansed from that area? Does that mean that their fears and premonitions were true, and also their objections to the effect that you could not protect them? Weren't they right to believe that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again my testimony points to a sequence of events and counter-events. At certain points, both sides, the Serbs and the Croats, got us into a hopeless situation of who started what, and what was the cause and what was the reaction? So if you mention those major events, yes, I testified, for example, in January or thereabouts that Croatians took action at Maslenica Bridge, attacking that, but the Croats also pointed to us that bridge in Maslenica was being held by the Serbs from a previous occasion. So every one of the events that you mentioned end up being a counterpoint from somebody else's point of view. Now, to come to the bottom line of your question, you claim the UN failed to protect. I come back to the same point again: The nature of the mission was for everyone, inclusive of the Serbs, to demobilise, lay back, and let the UN observe civilian police keep law and order while there was a political solution being found. We know that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's another question here, Mr. Kirudja. Since you say that some thought one thing or did one thing and others thought or did the other thing, is it being contested that these attacks of the Croat forces were against areas that were protected by the UN?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The attack on Sector West that we referred to was an area under the UN protection; correct. The eventual attack that ended up with the occupation of all those sectors, you're correct; it was undertaken by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to what you said in court yesterday. Truth to tell, some of it is in your written statement as well. Is it correct, because you mentioned that the Serbs did carry out the Vance Plan, and in accordance with this plan, they did indeed put all their heavy weapons under double lock, as you had put it yourself. That is to say, under their own control and UN control together. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My testimony was up to a period of time that happened, and later on, the weapons were retrieved from the UN custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us see what the reasons for that were, Mr. Kirudja. The weapons were put under control, the plan was carried out, and the weapons were taken after these attacks when they established that you could not protect them, that they had to protect themselves. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion itself, the sequence of the facts is correct. The fact that the attacks -- the conclusion that the attacks, when they established that the UN could not protect them, meaning could not protect the Serbs, that is not correct, because as I said, there were obligations on the Serb side not to militarise that situation. If you look at the evidence itself, they went there and took all that weapons as soon as an action as far as away as Maslenica, if you look at where Maslenica is, it's way down from Sector North. The Serbs went in in Sector North and took out all the weapons out of Sector North, far away from the where the action had taken place. Now, you may be right partially that they did fear that something would happen. That I concede. But with the presence of the UN, one would have expected, like every other disturbance that took place, we came into negotiation and had a pull-back. We have shown testimony after testimony where the Serbs themselves incurred way into Bosnia-Herzegovina, like in Bosanska Bojna. The Bosnian army didn't invade the sector. We worked until we had a solution and the Serbs pulled back. There was no reason why this wouldn't have been done after the initial attack in Maslenica. The UN didn't get a chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's an assumption, Mr. Kirudja, but now let's look at the facts. You said yourself that they put this under control, under double lock, and it was only taken in January 1993 as a result of the action that the Croat forces had taken. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that this is a UNPA. They handed in their weapons. The weapons were under double lock. The Croat forces attacked, and they opened these arms depots in order to take the weapons and protect themselves. Do you believe that this is a logical type of behaviour on the part of persons who are in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. Milosevic, because as I mentioned, the action that was the reason for breaking into the UN control of those weapons took place far away. It was Maslenica. Yes, I also conceded to you that, yes, while that may have cause for some future fear, it was not a reason for immediate running down of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But then -- I mean, whether it was a reason or not, it is a question of assessment at a given point in time. Now, you say further on that in April 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was peaceful, and that in May 1992 there had already been problems. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know how the first clashes started in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First in -- Mr. Milosevic, in what sense first? What time line are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying that there was the Cutilheiro plan, and before the Cutilheiro plan, there had been no clashes. There had been no bloodshed. All three ethnic communities believed that there would be a political solution that would peaceful, and you claim that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was peaceful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over the Cutilheiro plan. The witness has not been able to answer any questions. So I don't think there's any point going back again over this old ground. If you want to ask about the protected zones, of course you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kirudja, that the Croat formations from the territory of Croatia broke in in March 1992? I'll give you the exact date. I haven't got the exact figures here now, but I can give it to you eventually. Perhaps you may recall yourself. They broke into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the area of the municipality of Bosanski Brod, and they then killed a large number of Serb families in the village of Sijekovac, and that that was the first armed act of violence and crime in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina committed precisely then by the forces that had crossed the river into the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many reports I heard, not always -- and that one being away from my sector and the refugees themselves not coming through the sector, I'm afraid, Mr. Milosevic, the details of that are not known to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about this, how the first clashes in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. The witness has said he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the testimony itself, then. You talk about your discussion with General Spiro Nikovic in Topusko, and you say that he informed you that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been established, that from then onwards, the JNA would have no influence whatsoever in Bosnia, and that officers and soldiers who were not from Bosnia or Croatia would return to Yugoslavia. Did that actually happen?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting with Nikovic where this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting did take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, was this actually carried through, then, that the JNA withdrew to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified here, General Nikovic gave his counterpart, General Bamaiyi, a complete schedule of what and when JNA -- of when JNA units would be withdrawn. He was himself -- his command was terminated. In a few weeks, that command was finished, but he did -- the control of the parts of the sector that comprised Kordun, Banija, and Plaski did come under the control of officers of the kind he described, those who were born there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. So does that mean that, in your assessment, people spoke to you openly, that you were given correct figures? You even mentioned that you were taken to command posts, that you had the opportunity of going wherever you wished, and that their behaviour towards you was fair and correct and that they actually carried out the tasks that they promised they would carry out. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right that we were permitted to meet without restrictions. Wherever the meetings were supposed to be, we went out restriction. You are correct that their behaviour towards us as UN forces was correct and helpful in trying to achieve. The results themselves, it's your assessment to make, they are as described. The outcome is as described. Specifically, JNA disappeared in name. There was no name JNA. The command -- since you know the area, more specifically, Kordun remained under the control of Cedo Bulat, which it was before we arrived, and which it remained after the JNA. It was still under the control of Colonel Bulat. Banija remained under the control, or shifted several times before it finally came under the control of Colonel Tarbuk beginning with Rakovic, Letic, and a few others who were in command for a very short time, and I assume or was explained, rather, for example, Rakovic, was from Montenegro, so he too left. So Banija also ended up being under the control of Colonel Tarbuk. But Colonel Tarbuk was there when we arrived, and the JNA. As a matter of fact, he has reported in my notes underneath the first meeting when General Nambiar arrived. So we have them commanding the same military structure but with the name Banija Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and so forth. So while the JNA disappeared, the command structure was basically the same, stayed the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpreter to finish interpreting what you had just said. But tell me, please, Mr. Kirudja, what was the conclusion that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. drew from that? Or let me be more precise: During the time of the former Yugoslavia, the only army was the Yugoslav People's Army; is that right? That is something that is not being contested. When the civil war broke out and the violent secession of Slovenia first and then Croatia in these premature recognitions and so on and so forth, practically all the armies that were established - that which was in the FRY and that which was in Croatia, in Croatia and in Krajina, in Slovenia and in Bosnia, both in Izetbegovic's Bosnia and in Republika Srpska - all of them in a way were former parts of the former Yugoslav People's Army. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. They were a former part of the Yugoslav army structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is strange about that? Namely, that part of the members of the former Yugoslav People's Army who were from that area established the armed forces of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, or the police of the Republic of Serb Krajina, just as, for example, the officers and the armed forces of the former JNA from the territory of Croatia established the Croatian forces, or Izetbegovic's army where the officers and the troops that were part of the JNA established their own forces. However, they also included Mujahedin terrorists and many others. And this did not happen anywhere else but there. Is that the process that was taking place there or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised, Mr. Milosevic, you ask me that question because there lies the rub, because you know the Vance Plan required there be no forces in that area, and you know the details of it. It also required that only police be in the UNPA. Thirdly, it was required there be no such thing as the Republic of Srpska Krajina as a government. You know that. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the point: Didn't you come to the conclusion yourself that it was the police that remained ultimately, with reinforcements, in all fairness. But whoever was there until January 1993, until the attack; namely, weapons were handed in to the UN, the Vance Plan was carried out, and it was only the police that was there on the ground. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Kirudja? Everything that was -- I mean, everything and everybody that was on the ground was the police; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, that's what I belaboured to be accurate about. We expected not just they stay there from August to January of 1993, and you know that the Vance Plan expected them to be there as long as there was no political solution found under ICFY. So that itself was a violation of the Vance Plan, the act you so accurately describe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, I wonder if there's much point arguing more with the witness about this matter. He has given his account. We have heard what you say happened, and no doubt we shall have to make our minds up in due course as to where the truth lies, but the witness has given his evidence that, as far as he was concerned, this behaviour amounted to a violation of the plan. You claim there was an explanation for it. We will have to consider that. But whether we're going to benefit any more from lengthy argument with the witness about it, I rather doubt. Now, the time has in fact come where we're going to have to adjourn. So perhaps you can go on to another topic tomorrow morning. I should say that we've considered the time that you should have available, and you will have an equality with the Prosecution, which means that you have one and a half hours left tomorrow morning to conclude your cross-examination of this witness, should you require it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure, Mr. May, that that one and a half hours will be sufficient for me. There are many documents that were provided in relation to Mr. Kirudja's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, throughout this trial that there are time limits which will be imposed, and when you organise your cross-examination, you should have that in mind. Partly that is why you're being told that you have an hour and a half left and you can organise your cross-examination accordingly. But one of the lessons you should draw from it is not to argue with the witness and not to try and ask him about things which he knows nothing about. Thereby, you'll use your time more usefully. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
